newsitem.title: USA: Collectors finding value in those old beer cans.
newsitem.headline: Collectors finding value in those old beer cans.

text.p: An important day in history for a special segment of the collecting population is January 24, 1935: the day beer was first sold in cans.
Let the collecting begin.
Full cans, empties, cone tops or flat tops, aluminum or steel, if there's a can in your garage -- a likely storage place for many, collectors say -- it may be of some value.

Steel cans are the most valuable if they were produced before 1960 and were in cone top-shaped cans. Cone top cans were used mostly by smaller breweries because they could be filled on the existing bottle lines and the company would not have to invest in expensive new equipment.

Aluminum cans will never carry the same high values because millions are made annually and the quality of the colouring and design is not as good as the old steel cans that sometimes carried up to eight different colours, according to Bill Mugrage, author of the "Price Guide To Beer Cans, 5th Edition".
Mugrage says there are two pricing categories above individual can values; exotic and unique. An exotic can is rare and worth about $600 to $1,200. Any damage to these cans greatly affects the value.
A unique can is worth over $1,200 and he says there are probably less than a dozen mint-condition cans of this type in circulation.

Even a rusty can that you may toss in the trash has its own category -- dumpers. These are cans found outdoors with quite a bit of damage. But because of their rarity or other reasons, they will carry a value of between 5 and 25 percent, or, in rare cases, 50 percent, of mint condition value. Mugrage said these should not be overlooked in a collection.

"Although a really rare can probably hasn't been thrown away for more than 20 years, there are still some out there," said Mugrage. "The demise of the small brewery in the '50s and '60s, the introduction of aluminum cans in the early '70s and the increase in returnable cans have all contributed to the decline in outdoor dumping."
Over the years, millions of speciality and regular line beer cans have been produced. A few have skyrocketed in value.
For example, Sacramento, Calif.'s Buffalo Brewing Inc. has a single-label, 12-ounce, flat top, gold can listed in the exotic price range.

National Brewing Co. of Phoenix produced James Bond's 007 Special Blend beer. There were two sets of seven cans each and the labels on both pictured beautiful women and various London attractions. If you have one, it's worth about $250.
The Boston Beer Co.'s 12-ounce cans of Boston Light Ale and Boston Stock Ale have a value ranging from $150 to $400.

The G. Kruger Brewing Co. in Newark, N.J. -- the first company to sell beer in a can -- has cans ranging from $40 for a Krueger A Premium Cream Ale, to $200 for a Krueger Finest Beer single label, 12-ounce flat top to a Krueger's Special Beer, a red, 12-ounce, flat top with its "k-man" on gold rectangle in the unique price category.

Sports fans who collect cans honouring their favourite teams have not been left out. Pittsburgh Brewing Co.'s Iron City produced a plethora of speciality cans, including a 12-ounce tab top, single label, "1979 World Champion Pirates"; various cans celebrating football's "Super Steelers" and "Stanley Cup Champions" series for the NHL's Penguins. However, most of those types of cans from any brewery are fairly common and generally command all of $5.

If political cans line your mantle, Esslinger's Inc. of Philadelphia issued nine sets of "quiz cans" from 1953-1964 that have eight rows of text or facts on them. It is probably the only beer can where you'll find this mini-fact: "25th President William H. Taft" -- the price range is $75-$125.

More recently, Presidential Bottlers Inc. in Cleveland has been supplying thirsty collectors in at least 12 states with their "Dolelightful" and "Billary" beers in time for the 1996 election. Company President David Kaufmann said they also bottled a "BossRoss" brew, but billionaire candidate Ross Perot was not amused and his humourless lawyers threatened legal action, so production was halted.
For collectors wondering if he at least saved any cans of "BossRoss", Kaufman said it "wasn't worth the (legal) risk to us."

Tom Bates of Goodlettsville, Tenn., who began collecting beer cans as a child, takes his hobby seriously -- at last count he had 36,000 cans. When he and his father could no longer store them on their property, they opened the Museum of Beverage Containers and Advertising in 1987.
"The older cans hold their value," Bates said. "It may be better than collecting coins or stamps.

Without revealing values, he said many of his prized assets were acquired by "dumping" -- scavenging back roads where people used to toss their garbage. The day the family found a coveted 007 can, he said they "just stood there in silence."

The best places to search for valuable old cans are old buildings, especially abandoned farm houses, hunting cabins, barns and even outhouses. Flea markets, antique stores and collector magazines also should not be overlooked.

"The older and rarer the can, the more the potential buyer will be critical of any damage, including nicks and scratches. General cleaning and fixing of minor defects, if done properly, will enhance the value of a can," according to Mugrage's book. "Cans with holes are of little value.
"The value of aluminum cans will, at some point, reach a ceiling, while steel cans will continue to rise in value."

Prices quoted are almost always for cans in mint condition -- meaning no scratches, dents, rust or staining of any kind. Beer can values, like those of other collectibles, are determined by demand, the book said. The famous Rosalie can that sold for more than $6,000 in the late '70s would be greatly reduced in value if even a perfect six-pack was found.
Beer can lovers have formed the Beer Can Collectors of America. Their annual "Canvention" is Sept. 18-21 in Indianapolis.
